footer: Full-course recap for DSM-107 Managerial Economics. Micro part S01–S10, macro part S11–S20 (Prof. Deepak Sethia). Built from the lecture notes in lectures/. Every GDP total, multiplier, money multiplier, bond price, real exchange rate and parity rate on this page was recomputed from the lecture's own numbers. The widgets replay the lecture's examples: the farmer–baker economy, the wheat/potato GDP table, the ₹1,000 crore project, the 1,000 → 5,000 deposit-creation chain, the iPhone/furniture real-exchange-rate cases, the 50 → 55 interest-parity example and the 3% wage-round story.
course_notes: EXTENSION: modules m7–m13 cover the macro half (S11–S20, all Prof. Deepak Sethia; S10 was the last micro session). The existing m1–m6 (micro, S01–S10) are not repeated. Cross-links are allowed: the sectoral-shift examples in m7/m13 echo opportunity cost (m1); trade-driven price convergence in m11 echoes comparative advantage (m2); coordination failure and competitive devaluation (m12/m13) may point back to the social dilemmas in m5. Central contrast for the macro modules: amber = nominal / money / financial (rupees, printed notes, nominal GDP, nominal interest and exchange rates, nominal wages); teal = real (goods and services, output, jobs, real GDP, real rate, real exchange rate). The instructor's refrains are 'the financial sector is the servant; the real economy is the master' (S16), 'we are ultimately interested in goods and services' (S18) and 'more money does not create more real goods' (S15). A second recurring contrast sits inside teal: short run (demand-driven, use of existing capacity) vs long run (supply-driven, capacity; growth is not covered). If the existing page legend differs, keep the page's legend and apply this amber/teal mapping within m7–m13. Units: rupees (₹, lakh, crore) throughout; USD for US data, forex and BoP (USD bn). Exchange rates are quoted in ₹ per $. The instructor uses ₹50/$ for simplicity, says the actual rate is about ₹96, and expects to switch to ₹100. No exam-format statements appear in S11–S20. Chat polls were used to record attendance (S14). Repo, reverse repo, CRR and SLR were flagged for interview preparation (S16). Slides (PPT) were promised (S20). Never name students. ASR fixes to apply: Keynesian cross, HDFC, MGNREGA, PM-Kisan Samman Nidhi, Ladli Behna, Mewar, Dussehra. KaTeX is OFF on this page (it uses $ for dollars): write formulas in <code>, never $...$.

modules.plan:
Module 'What macro studies, and measuring GDP' (S11–S12). Content type: numerical (accounting identities), with framework cards.

CHEAT CARDS:
- Macro = aggregates: all markets hit together in a recession, unlike sectoral shifts.
- Long run vs short run table: trend is supply-driven (capital, infrastructure, human capital, technology) = growth, not covered. Fluctuations are demand-driven = this course. India per-capita growth is about 4%/yr.
- Potential output, actual output, output gap.
- GDP definition with its highlighted terms: market value, final goods and services, factors of production, within borders.
- Output ≡ income ≡ expenditure.
- Circular-flow legend: dashed = real flows, solid = money; blue = factor flows, red = final demand, black = transfers (taxes, saving, PM-Kisan / Ladli Behna). Factor payments: land→rent, labour→wages, capital→interest, entrepreneurship→profit. Adding all red flows (C + I + G + NX) = adding all blue payments.
- GVA = GVO − IC. Count final goods only; intermediate goods are embedded in the final good. GVA ≠ profit (it is wages + rent + interest + profit).
- Imputation rule: self-produced goods count at market price; imputed rent counts; paid domestic help counts; home services do not count.
- Inventory valued at the cost of work done this year (₹18, not ₹20). Selling activity counts next year.
- Perished output: all incomes count, including negative profit.
- Three approaches: expenditure C+I+G+X−M; production ΣGVA + net production taxes; income Σ factor incomes + net indirect taxes.
- GDP at market prices = GDP at factor cost + indirect taxes − subsidies.
- I = fixed + inventory (planned and unplanned). The same car or laptop is C or I depending on use. G is valued at cost of production.
- NDP = GDP − depreciation (consumption of fixed capital, including obsolescence).
- GNP is by residency of the factor owner, not citizenship. Remittances are current transfers, not factor income.
- Saving–investment identity: S_h = (Y − T + TR − C) = I + (G + TR − T) + (X − M), with the twin-deficit implication.
- Exclusions: financial transactions, second-hand goods (margin only), transfers, gifts, illegal activity.

NOTES / ANALOGIES:
- Great Depression, two scenarios: factories vanished vs factories and workers idle because firms feared they could not sell; the answer is the second. Contrast with India's development problem of missing capacity (S11).
- Sectoral shifts are not macro: Ola/Uber/Rapido vs autos, landlines→mobiles, diet changes. 'Probably don't bail out the declining sector' (S11).
- Sometimes not intervening is the better choice (S11).
- Mukesh Ambani 'belongs to the Antilia household' and supplies labour to Reliance (S11).
- Ambani minding his grandkids: which wage would you impute? Hence home services are excluded (S11).
- Government university fee ₹1,000/yr, school ₹500–1,000: economically insignificant prices; the extra unit is not decided by price (S11).
- Refinery: crude $100 → product $105, value added $5 (S11).
- Apples ₹20/kg in Himachal vs ₹80 in Indore: moving goods to consumers is value added; this is why unsold bread is ₹18 (S11).
- GDP ignores distribution: 100 people eating 10 kg each vs one eating 1,000 kg (S11).
- Correction from class: the baker's 250 is not profit (S11).
- Cliff-hanger on perishable bread, resolved in S12 by double entry: 15 + 3 − 18 = 0 (S12).
- Owner-occupier imputed rent; tax authorities deem rent on a third house (S12).
- Maruti builds stock in April–July for the festive season (planned inventory) (S12).
- Surgery costs ₹1 lakh privately vs ₹3,000–5,000 in a government hospital, so G is valued at cost (S12).
- iPhone: C = 80,000, M = 70,000, Y = 10,000. Tata Nano exported to South Africa: X = 1 lakh (S12).
- Lecture at Harvard: US GDP, India GNP. Maruti dividends to Suzuki: Japan's GNP. Ireland/Iceland have large GDP–GNP gaps (S12).
- UAE remittances are gifts-like transfers (S12).
- Why GDP not NDP for macro: all ₹1,500 cr of investment creates jobs this year, replacement or not (S12).
- Twin deficits 1975–1990s: the lecturer argues the fiscal deficit, not the CAD, was the root of the 1991 crisis (S12).
- Matchmaker income counts; samosa sellers and barbers are estimated from consumption surveys; MGNREGA is not a pure transfer because work is done (S12).

ONE WIDGET 'Farmer–baker GDP ledger':
- Fixed: wheat 50 kg at ₹15; bread ₹20; the baker's ₹5 split = ₹3 conversion + ₹2 selling (from S12).
- Sliders: kg of wheat self-consumed s (0–50); bread sold q (0 to 50 − s). Unsold u = 50 − s − q. Toggle perishable / non-perishable.
- Three side-by-side columns that must agree:
  - Expenditure: 15s + 20q + (non-perishable ? 18u : 0).
  - Production: 750 + 5q + 3u, minus 18u if perishable.
  - Income: farmer 750 + conversion 3(50 − s) + selling 2q + baker loss (−18u if perishable).
- Presets: (a) all sold = 1,000; (b) self-consumption = 900; (c) 10 unsold, non-perishable = 880; (d) 10 unsold, perishable = 700.
- Verdict line names the trap avoided. (a) 'not 1,750 — no double counting'. (b) 'not 600 — impute self-consumption'. (c) 'inventory at 18 not 20'. (d) 'the baker's −180 keeps income = expenditure'.
- Expose window.__recap.m7.ledger(s, q, perishable).

WORKED PROBLEMS:

2. The perishable-bread reconciliation.

modules.facts: Apple economy: 100 apples × ₹1 = 100; wages 70 + profit 30 = 100; uses C 60 + G 10 + I 30 = 100 (the lecture once said 'buy back 70, save 30', omitting G — slip). Farmer–baker: wheat 50 × 15 = 750; bread 50 × 20 = 1000; wrong double count 750 + 1000 = 1750; baker VA 1000 − 750 = 250; shares 750/1000 = 75%, 250/1000 = 25%; per unit 20 − 15 = 5, 50 × 5 = 250. Refinery 105 − 100 = 5. Self-consumption: expenditure 30×20 + 20×15 = 600 + 300 = 900; production 750 + 30×5 = 750 + 150 = 900 (wrong student answer 600). Inventory (non-perishable): 300 + 20×20 + 10×(15+3) = 300 + 400 + 180 = 880; production 750 + 20×5 + 10×3 = 880 (cross-check not in S11, implied in S12). Perishable: 300 + 400 = 700; per kg 15 + 3 − 18 = 0; total 880 − 10×18 = 700. Widget income formula check: (a) 750 + 3×50 + 2×50 = 1000; (b) 750 + 3×30 + 2×30 = 900; (c) 750 + 90 + 40 = 880; (d) 880 − 180 = 700. Pizza chain: 23 + (53−23) + (110−53) + (200−110) = 23 + 30 + 57 + 90 = 200; with 5% GST 200 × 1.05 = 210. Mobile: 6000 + 3000 + 1000 = 10,000 at factor cost; market price 10,000 + 2,000 − 500 = 11,500; GDP at factor cost 3,000 + 1,000 = 4,000; C − M = 11,500 − 6,000 = 5,500 = 4,000 + 2,000 − 500. iPhone 80,000 − 70,000 = 10,000. Nano X = 1,00,000. Net investment 1,500 − 600 = ₹900 crore. Disposable income 100 − 30 + 10 = 80. Twin-deficit chart: household saving about +1.3 pp, investment about +0.9 pp (approximate, read from chart). India per-capita growth about 4%/yr over four decades. Fees: university ₹1,000/yr, school ₹500–1,000/yr; surgery ₹1 lakh private vs ₹3,000–5,000 government. Apples ₹20/kg Himachal vs ₹80/kg Indore. Residency test >183 days.

modules.plan:
Module 'Nominal vs real, price indices, and who loses from inflation' (S12 end – S13 first half). Content type: numerical.

CHEAT CARDS:
- Nominal GDP_t = Σ P_t Q_t (current prices); real GDP_t = Σ P_b Q_t (constant base-year prices). Prices are the weights because you can't add apples and oranges.
- g_nominal ≈ g_real + π. Newspaper growth figures are always real.
- CPI as a weighted average of price relatives with base-year expenditure shares, which equals the Laspeyres ratio Σ P_t Q_b / Σ P_b Q_b. Explain the numerator and denominator in words.
- π_t = (CPI_t − CPI_{t−1}) / CPI_{t−1} × 100. RBI target 4% ± 2%.
- CPI vs WPI: retail goods + services vs wholesale goods only. WPI is the early-warning signal.
- Fisher: 1 + r = (1 + i)/(1 + π), r ≈ i − π^e. Unexpected inflation redistributes from lenders to borrowers.
- Base year rules: a normal year, as recent as possible. Revisions 2004–05 → 2011–12 → 2022–23 (Feb 2026).
- Per capita, not total, GDP for welfare; income is a flow, wealth is a stock.
- Single vs double deflation (debated; the lecturer leans to single for manufacturing).
- CPI basket built from the NSO consumption survey; it differs across states.

NOTES / ANALOGIES:
- Income ₹50,000 → ₹1.5 lakh looks like a tripling, but prices rose 50–70% (S12).
- 'The base year is very crucial' (S13).
- Avoid 2020 (COVID), 2016–17 (demonetisation) and 2017–18 (GST) as base years (S13).
- A 512 MB pen drive cost ₹2,000–3,000 in 2006–08. Valuing today's drives at old prices makes people look implausibly rich (S13).
- Grandparents' land and wooden furniture vs today's ACs and fridges can't be compared (S13).
- WPI leads CPI because printed menus and MRPs change only with the next batch (S13).
- If all prices rise 10%, incomes rise 10% too; the medical-product maker is indifferent (S13).
- 'A subtle point but a very important point': food-led inflation plus DA. The rich spend about 15% on food, the poor about 50%. The indexed rich get DA for inflation that hits others and spend it on iPads. Maids and drivers are not indexed, so inflation is regressive (S13).
- Lend ₹100 for ₹110, chocolates and the toffee-factory borrower: expected 6% vs actual 12% (S13).
- Single vs double deflation compared to Coca-Cola vs Thums Up (S13).
- CPI Kerala vs Bihar (food weight), Mumbai (rent weight), betel leaf in Assam (S13).
- Per capita ₹285 at 1950 prices vs about ₹13,000 at 2011–12 prices; only the constant-price figure is meaningful (S13).

WIDGET 1 'Nominal vs real GDP' (wheat and potato, base 2010):
- Year buttons 2010 / 2011 / 2013. Table shows Q and P for each good, nominal GDP, real GDP at 2010 prices, and the ratio nominal/real.
- Bar pair (amber nominal, teal real) on one scale.
- Readout decomposes the change into a volume factor × a price factor. Verdict: '2011: nominal doubled, real unchanged — pure inflation'; '2013: 16 = 4 volume × 4 price'.
- Expose window.__recap.m8.gdp(year).

WIDGET 2 'Lender vs borrower':
- Sliders: nominal rate i (0–15%), expected inflation π^e, actual inflation π (0–15%).
- Readouts: what ₹110 buys versus ₹100 today, exact real return (1+i)/(1+π) − 1, Fisher approximation i − π.
- Verdict names who gains: teal 'lender earns about 4% real' at the 6% preset; amber 'borrower gains, lender loses about 1.8%' at the 12% preset.
- Presets: (10, 6, 6) and (10, 6, 12).

WORKED PROBLEMS:
1. Reproduce 200 → 3200 nominal and 200 → 800 real.
2. Real return at 10% nominal with 6% vs 12% inflation, exact and approximate.
3. Explain in words why food-led inflation plus DA is regressive.
modules.facts: Wheat/potato (2011 prices inferred from 'prices doubled'; 2012 not read out): 2010 nominal 10×10 + 5×20 = 200; 2011 nominal 10×20 + 5×40 = 400, real 10×10 + 5×20 = 200; 2013 nominal 40×40 + 20×80 = 1600 + 1600 = 3200, real 40×10 + 20×20 = 800; 3200/200 = 16 = 4 × 4; 800/200 = 4; implied price ratio 3200/800 = 4 (derived, not stated). Growth rule: real 7–7.5% + inflation 4–5% ≈ 11–12.5% (the lecturer said both 'nominal ~14–15%' and '~12%' — inconsistent). Income 50,000 → 1,50,000 (×3); prices +50–70% → real 3/1.5 = 2.0 to 3/1.7 ≈ 1.76 (the lecture said about 1.5–2×). RBI target 4 ± 2 → 2% to 6%. Fisher: 110/106 − 1 = 0.0377 (≈ 3.8%, 'close to 4%'), approx 10 − 6 = 4%; 110/112 − 1 = −0.0179 (≈ −1.8%), approx 10 − 12 = −2%. Food shares: rich ₹10,000–15,000 of ₹1,00,000 ≈ 15%; poor ₹4,000–5,000 of ₹10,000 ≈ 40–50% (the lecture says about 50%). Spending-share illustration: 25p health, 25p education, 20p food, 10p rent per ₹1. Per capita GDP 1950–51: ₹285 current, ≈ ₹13,000 at 2011–12 prices; 2021–22 about 8–9× in real terms. Base years 2004–05, 2011–12, 2022–23 (revision Feb 2026). NSO survey about 1.5 lakh households. Pen drive 512 MB ₹2,000–3,000 (2006–08).

modules.plan:
Module 'Sticky prices, the Keynesian cross and the multiplier' (S13 second half, S14, S15 part A). Content type: derivation / numerical.

CHEAT CARDS:
- Potential output Y*; frictional unemployment about 4–5% even at full employment.
- Why firms cut output, not prices: customer habituation; wages rigid downward. Hence a flat SRAS with unemployment and an AD-driven cycle (Keynes).
- Consumption C = C̄ + cY (largest AD component: about 60% India, 70% US). Determinants: income, future prospects, pensions, interest, age. S = Y − C.
- Y vs planned AD inventory rule (Y > AD → unplanned accumulation → cut; Y < AD → depletion → raise; Y = AD equilibrium, S = I).
- Keynesian cross: the 45° line has tan 45° = 1, so height = base. AD = Ā + cY, flatter than 45°.
- Ā = C̄ − cTA + cTR + Ī + Ḡ (lump-sum taxes).
- Multiplier 1/(1 − c), by equation and by GP sum a/(1 − r).
- Proportional tax: AD = Ā + c(1 − t)Y, multiplier 1/(1 − c(1 − t)) < 1/(1 − c) because c(1 − t) < c.
- Transfer and lump-sum tax multipliers = c·α_G (smaller, because the first round is skipped); ΔY = −c α_G ΔT.
- Raising t lowers AD and shrinks the multiplier.
- Budget surplus BS = tY − G − TR: intercept −(G + TR), slope t, so deficits widen automatically in bad times.
- Automatic stabilizers: income tax, unemployment benefit, MGNREGA.
- Pro- vs counter-cyclical fiscal policy.
- Equilibrium ≠ full employment.

NOTES / ANALOGIES:
- Potential is like your absorption just before exams: you can't sustain it 365 days (S13).
- Frictional examples: STD/PCO → delivery jobs; a locality switching from Chinese to Indian food (S13).
- Bernanke, Essays on the Great Depression (S13).
- A ₹5,000 product cut to ₹4,000 is hard to raise back (S13).
- Barber: ₹100 haircut, ₹3,000–5,000/month wage. Selling at ₹80 needs a wage cut workers refuse — 'easier to fire than cut wages' (S13).
- Highway → cement and steel → recalled workers at prevailing wages (S13–S15).
- COVID fresh juice and ice cream written off across firms = a macro, not micro, shock (S13).
- Festive inventories for Diwali, Dussehra and Ganesh Puja (S14).
- ₹1,000 crore factory → restaurant meals, shirts, holidays, round after round (S14).
- At full employment the highway only diverts cement from houses: reallocation plus inflation, no multiplier (S14).
- Repeated twice: 'Equilibrium only means whatever is produced is sold, not that whatever can be produced is produced' (S14).
- The instructor prefers a SMALLER multiplier because it also works in reverse (S14).
- ₹100 income example: 70 vs 28 — 'macro insurance' (S14).
- Discretionary policy is slow ('build the highway in my region'); stabilizers are automatic (S14).
- After the 1930s, tax and transfer systems made cycles milder (S14).
- 2008: Obama's direct spending ('buyer of last resort') vs useless roads and dying regions (S15).
- Procyclical policy copies household logic — 'earn less, spend less' is wrong for governments (S15).
- COVID borrowing; the DEA Secretary's case to rating agencies (S15).
- Two chat polls (bigger multiplier? better multiplier?) counted for attendance (S14).

ONE WIDGET 'Multiplier rounds':
- Inputs: injection ΔG = ₹1,000 crore (fixed); sliders MPC c (0.5–0.9) and tax rate t (0–0.4); toggle 'direct spending' vs 'transfer' (first round becomes c·ΔTR).
- Bars show rounds 1..12 (1000, 1000·c(1−t), ...), with a running cumulative line converging to the limit.
- Readouts: multiplier formula with numbers substituted, total ΔY.
- Presets: c = 2/3, t = 0 (rounds 1000, 667, 444, 296 → 3000); c = 0.8, t = 0 (×5); c = 0.8, t = 0.25 (×2.5, the S15 quiz); c = 0.8, t = 0.2 (×2.78, the notes' illustration — label 'not computed in class').
- Verdict: 'a 25% tax halves the multiplier from 5 to 2.5'. In transfer mode: 'transfers skip the first round'.
- A note under the widget says the multiplier needs idle resources.
- Expose window.__recap.m9.alpha(c, t).

STATIC: a labelled Keynesian-cross figure showing E1 below Y* and the AD shift from higher G; the ₹100 stabilizer table; the procyclical/countercyclical three-curve sketch.

WORKED PROBLEMS:
1. ₹1,000 crore at MPC 2/3 by equation and by GP.
2. α_G at c = 0.8, t = 0.25.
3. The ₹100 stabilizer example (70 vs 49 − 21 = 28).
modules.facts: Simple multiplier c = 0.8: 1/(1 − 0.8) = 1/0.2 = 5. MPC 2/3 rounds: 1000, 1000×2/3 = 666.7 (lecture '≈666'), 1000×(2/3)^2 = 444.4, 1000×(2/3)^3 = 296.3; sum = 1000/(1 − 2/3) = 3000 crore. Proportional tax c = 0.8, t = 0.25 (parameters implied by the class answer 2.5): 1/(1 − 0.8×0.75) = 1/(1 − 0.6) = 1/0.4 = 2.5 vs 5. Illustration c = 0.8, t = 0.2: c(1−t) = 0.64, 1/0.36 ≈ 2.78 (in notes, not computed in class). Transfer multiplier c·α_G: e.g. 0.8 × 2.5 = 2.0; 2/3 × 3 = 2.0 (derived from the formula; no number given in class). Stabilizer example, MPC 0.7: no tax 100 × 0.7 = 70 → loss 70; with 30% tax and ₹30 benefit, employed (100 − 30) × 0.7 = 49, unemployed 30 × 0.7 = 21, loss 49 − 21 = 28. Budget surplus BS = tY − G − TR, intercept −(G + TR), slope t. Consumption share of GDP about 60% India, 70% US. Frictional unemployment about 4–5%. Barber: haircut ₹100, wage ₹3,000–5,000/month, cut price ₹80. Habituation ₹5,000 → ₹4,000. Factory ₹1,000 crore.

modules.plan:
Module 'Money, banks, bonds and the RBI's tools' (S15 part B, S16, S17 first half). Content type: numerical, with case tables.

CHEAT CARDS:
- Money = a medium of exchange backed by belief that others accept it. Four functions: medium of exchange, store of value (imperfect under inflation), unit of account, standard of deferred payment. It is the most liquid asset.
- Commodity money (intrinsic value, real-resource cost) vs fiat money (trust, discipline; over-printing = inflation).
- M0 = high-powered money = monetary base = currency + reserves (H = CU + RE). M3 = broad money = currency + deposits (M = CU + D). The RBI creates only cash; commercial banks create deposits.
- Money multiplier mm = (1 + cu)/(cu + re), and M = mm × H.
- Comparative statics: lower re → larger mm; higher cu → smaller mm (because re < 1). Determinants of cu: ATMs, UPI, Diwali cash. re is set via the CRR plus excess reserves.
- Only banks create money, because their liabilities are a means of payment.
- Interbank logic table: surplus bank ↔ deficit bank; whole system short → borrow at the RBI window; whole system long → park at the RBI.
- Perpetual bond P = C/i, so bond prices and rates move inversely.
- 'Four statements, one event': RBI sells bonds = money supply falls = rates rise = bond prices fall.
- CRR changes the multiplier; OMO / repo change the base. Banks prefer repo because CRR earns nothing.
- Repo corridor: reverse repo ≤ WACR ≤ repo; 1 bp = 0.01%. Tight liquidity → WACR near the ceiling; surplus → near the floor.
- SLR = a captive market for government bonds (financial repression, reduced in 1991). CRR + SLR locked share.
- Bank balance sheet; loss order equity → debt → depositors; leverage; skin in the game.
- Bank run = self-fulfilling prophecy. Liquidity ≠ solvency. Lender of last resort; deposit insurance ₹5 lakh.
- Transmission: rate cut → investment demand ↑ → Ā ↑ → AD up toward Y*.

NOTES / ANALOGIES:
- A demonetised note still works as money if people accept it (S15).
- Barter: the professor needs a barber who wants an economics lecture (S15).
- Gold 1 g = ₹100 → declared ₹200: prices double. Like shrinkflation in a ₹10 noodle packet (S15).
- A ₹2,000 note's scrap value; 'I promise to pay the bearer' just means another note (S15).
- The ₹1 note is signed by the Finance Secretary; other notes by the RBI Governor (S15).
- Mughal silver and the Mewar trade route: 'if you don't control the trade route you don't control your currency'. Infosys/TCS export earnings locked in silver couldn't buy oil (S15).
- Zimbabwe: $1 bn held, $1 tn printed — printing = stealing from note-holders (S15).
- Crypto is like fiat without legal tender (S15).
- Say 'money available for transactions', never 'purchasing power' (S15).
- Don't use more UPI to 'get more money': more money ≠ more goods; helicopter money → inflation (S15).
- People trust the dollar, not Zimbabwean, Sri Lankan or Pakistani notes; the US left gold to print more (S15).
- The 200 in the vault can't buy toothpaste (S15).
- Tata Motors via SIP vs via bank deposit — only with the bank can both parties spend (S16).
- Gold bought 5 years ago sells at today's price, so an old ₹100/yr bond = a new one (S16).
- 'The financial sector is not the master; it is the servant. The real economy is the master' (S16).
- US base ×8–9 but M ×5: interest on reserves plus risk aversion — a central bank can't force banks to lend (S16).
- Demonetisation: currency → deposits, banks park the excess at the reverse repo, M0 falls, mm jumps, M unchanged (S16).
- Steel plant, grounded airlines, lockdown hotels, a COVID job loser — genuine defaults (S16).
- Feeling unwell because you believe you are — bank runs; forbearance for a job loser (S16).
- 'The government's collateral is its word' (S16).
- 'A Nobel laureate from outside may not be able to tell you what SLR is' (S16).
- 'Why is the dollar powerful? Basically, trust' (S16).
- Interview prep: know repo, reverse repo, CRR and SLR — 'just read the definitions' (S16).
- SBI asks HDFC 6% → HDFC borrows from the RBI at 5.75%; HDFC offers 5% → SBI parks at 5.25% (S17).
- 'The multiplier starts from Mumbai (RBI), not Delhi' (S17).
- 'The RBI wants you to take a housing loan in a recession' (S17).
- People hoard deposits at near-zero rates in 2008/COVID — precautionary saving (S17).

WIDGET 1 'Deposit-creation chain / money multiplier':
- Sliders: reserve ratio re (0.03–0.30) and currency ratio cu (0–0.5); base injection ΔH (1,000 or $40m preset).
- Shows round-by-round bars (deposit, kept as reserve, lent), the running M, and the closed-form limit.
- Presets: re = 0.2, cu = 0, ΔH = 1,000 → rounds 1000/800/640, M = 5,000, mm = 5. rr = 0.1, cr = 0.3, ΔB = $40m → mm = 3.25, ΔM = $130m.
- Readout states which ratio moved mm and why.
- Expose window.__recap.m10.mm(cu, re).

WIDGET 2 'Perpetual bond price':
- A ₹100/yr coupon and a market-rate slider i (4–16%) with the P = 100/i curve and a moving dot.
- Presets: 10% → ₹1,000; 8% → ₹1,250; 12% → ₹833 (the lecture said 'around 850').
- Caption chain: RBI sells bonds → price ↓ → i ↑ → money ↓.

STATIC: CRR vs OMO/repo table; corridor table with rates; SLR history table; balance sheet; India vs US multiplier cards.

WORKED PROBLEMS:

modules.plan:
Module 'Balance of payments, the forex market, real exchange rates and PPP' (S17 second half, S18). Content type: numerical + case tables.

CHEAT CARDS:
- Y = C + I + G + NX. Exports are added because domestic producers earn without C/I/G; imports are inside C and I but are not domestic output.
- Four distinct terms: BoP; current account (trade balance + NFI + net unilateral transfers); trade balance; capital account.
- 2×2 credit/debit vs current/capital matrix. Credit = forex in, debit = forex out.
- CA + KA = 0. Open-economy identity S = S_pvt + S_gov = Y + NFI + NUT − C − G, so S − I = CA.
- A CAD is judged by its source (rising I vs falling S) and by how the funds are used.
- Forex market: ₹/$ on the vertical axis. Down = rupee appreciation, up = depreciation. Dollar supply from exporters slopes up; dollar demand from importers slopes down.
- Fixed rate: an overvalued rupee (80 < 96) means excess dollar demand, RBI sells dollars = BoP deficit, unsustainable. An undervalued rupee (110 > 96) means RBI buys dollars = BoP surplus.
- BoP = CA + KA (including the RBI-reserve line). Under a pure float, BoP = 0.
- Regime words: devaluation/revaluation (fixed) vs depreciation/appreciation (flexible).
- India's history: fixed to 1971 (₹4.76 in 1949, 1966 devaluation), crawling step devaluations 1971–91, 1991 devaluation, flexible from about 1994–95, now a managed float with an undisclosed band.
- Real exchange rate ε = E·P_f/P_d: = 1 is PPP; < 1 is real appreciation (import more); > 1 is real depreciation (export more). Relative PPP: %ΔE ≈ π_d − π_f.
- PPP rate vs market rate: tradables vs non-tradables, plus tariffs and transport.
- Loanable funds: closed-economy crowding out. In an open economy i_d → i_f. Fiscal expansion → inflow → appreciation → CAD; higher government saving → outflow → depreciation → CA surplus.

NOTES / ANALOGIES:

- Tesla, an Anthropic IPO, Japanese metro/bullet-train funding, a Canadian pension fund — 'capital seeks the best return' (S17).
- A retiree breaking FDs or selling a house to fund spending (S17).

- Amul (pay in ₹) vs Hershey's (pay in $) (S17).

- 'Look at the forex market just like your plain microeconomics graphs' (S18).
- 'The one that can buy more of the other is appreciating' (S18).
- KEY 'read the last line carefully': don't ask why the rupee is depreciating, ask why our inflation differential is high (S18).
- Domestic help implies ₹5/$, a haircut ₹10/$; NRIs bring iPhones in and get haircuts and root canals here — 'you can't smuggle haircuts' (S18).
- An iPhone costs the same in Mumbai and Bhagalpur (S18).

modules.plan:
Module 'Policy in an open economy: fixed vs flexible, interest parity, the impossible trinity, India's BoP' (end of S18, S19 open-economy part). Content type: algorithmic (causal chains) + numerical.

CHEAT CARDS:
- NX = S − I with r = r* in a small open economy. Fiscal deficit → I > S → trade deficit; fiscal discipline → S > I → trade surplus.
- Policy result table under free capital mobility:
  - Fixed rate, monetary policy: ineffective (arbitrage forces i_d = i_f).
  - Fixed rate, fiscal policy: effective (accommodated by the RBI).
  - Flexible rate, monetary policy: effective via depreciation → NX → AD.
  - Flexible rate, fiscal policy: not covered in S19; the S18 loanable-funds case gives appreciation + CAD.
- Recession remedies: raise C, I, G or NX — money is not the only tool.
- Uncovered interest parity: exact 1 + i = (1 + i*)E^e/E; approx i ≈ i* + expected depreciation.
- Inflation differential → expected depreciation → interest differential. Risk premium is the second source.
- Impossible trinity (fixed rate, independent monetary policy, free capital mobility — choose two), with US/EU, Hong Kong, capital-control regimes and China's managed float.
- Euro = a fixed rate with one ECB rate. Members lose devaluation, which is the tool that gets around sticky nominal wages.
- Fixed vs flexible pros and cons; a fixed rate needs monetary discipline.
- BoP sign convention: a reserve increase is recorded as a negative entry.

NOTES / ANALOGIES:
- 'Delhi' spends and 'Mumbai' accommodates (S19).
- Lend to 100 people: one group with 1–2 defaults, another with 6–7 — charge the riskier group more. Pakistan, Nigeria; sudden tax hikes on foreigners (S19).
- India 7% vs US 5% means the market expects about 2% rupee depreciation a year. The gap fell from about 4 to 2 points because the inflation gap narrowed — that is not a reason to raise rates (S19).
- 'Let me be very clear': long-run exchange rates follow inflation differentials, so a stable rate needs inflation discipline (S19).
- Competitive devaluation = 'exporting unemployment'. Retaliation, trade wars and the world wars motivated European integration (S19).
- A French lender to a German is repaid in the same euros; a US lender to an Indian faces rupee risk (S19).
- India still restricts capital; the EU, Canada, Japan, US, Hong Kong and Singapore are highly mobile (S19).
- India's CAD is financed by capital inflows that depend on foreigners' confidence (S19).

modules.plan:
Module 'Aggregate supply, unemployment, the Phillips curve, expectations and stabilisation' (S19 second part, S20). Content type: mostly framework (cards and tables) plus one algorithmic stepper for the expectations story. Do not chart the frameworks.

CHEAT CARDS:
- SRAS horizontal (Keynesian, sticky wages, idle workers) vs LRAS vertical at Y* (capital, technology, labour), shifting right only through capacity growth. Flagged: 'need to understand this very clearly'.
- Micro vs macro elasticity reversal table: micro is inelastic in the short run and elastic in the long run; macro is flat in the short run and vertical in the long run. Reason: relative demand vs demand for everything at once.
- Market speeds: asset markets fast, goods markets slower, labour slowest.
- L = N + U, u = U/(N + U). Zero unemployment is neither feasible nor desirable.
- Unemployment types: frictional (higher with generous benefits), structural (skill/sector mismatch), cyclical (output < Y*; the macro target). Full employment = frictional + structural only.
- Realistic AS: flat → upward → near-vertical.
- Voluntary vs involuntary unemployment on the labour-market graph with a sticky W*.
- Eight reasons for stickiness: labour contracts, other nominal contracts, misperception, menu costs, coordination failure, insider/outsider, hiring/firing costs, efficiency wages.
- Phillips curve (A.W. Phillips, UK 1861–1913): convex, a short-run trade-off.
- Wage hike = productivity growth + π^e. The height of the Phillips curve = expected inflation. NAIRU. Inflation inertia (Solow).
- Inflation is the rate of change of the price level; zero inflation means stable prices, not falling ones.
- Disinflation needs a recession (Volcker); credibility lowers the cost — three scenarios.
- Anticipated vs unanticipated inflation: the real wage and real loan arithmetic.
- Why deflation is worse: sticky wages, postponed spending, the zero lower bound.
- Targets: RBI 4% ± 2%; US/Europe 2%.
- Three ways to finance a deficit: print money, borrow domestically (crowding out), borrow abroad (future CA surplus). Burden on future generations; crowding in below full employment.
- Closing line: stabilise output at potential on either side; at full employment, hold the status quo. Pro/counter-cyclical policy is already in m9 — just cross-reference it.

NOTES / ANALOGIES:
- Berozgari and mehngai, the two perpetual electoral issues (S19).
- Pulses/milk demand rising draws resources from other sectors; when everything rises together, all firms bid for the same workers (S19).
- An RBI cut moves bond markets immediately, cement demand with a lag, hiring last (S19).

- Shared mobility moves car workers to driving; millets move farmers between crops (S19).
- Workers suspect the employer is 'bluffing' about a recession; they refuse the cut, discover the recession, then accept (S20).
- Textile producer fooled by its own price signal; a worker who later finds ₹10,000 buys less, then asks for ₹11,000 (S20).
- Restaurant onion/tomato spikes don't reprint the menu (S20).
- Insiders bargain, outsiders aren't at the table (S20).
- The unemployed pool disciplines shirkers and reduces HR monitoring (S20).
- Politicians read the Phillips curve as a menu (S20).
- 'Expectations translate into reality' — the 4% self-fulfilling wage round (S20).
- 'You can create demand by printing notes, but you cannot create supply' (S20).
- Volcker: short rates 14–15%, mortgages 16–17%, nobody buys houses (S20).
- 'The labour market is tight' = rates will rise (S20).
- Disinflation is a 'cruel' trade-off (S20).
- Governor: 10% past inflation, 2% promised (S20).
- Seigniorage: a ₹2,000 note costs ₹5–10 to print — why a central bank might bluff (S20).
- Traffic rules: if the police drive on the wrong side, or fines are never levied, credibility collapses (S20).
- At 25% inflation a ±5 error is costly; '15% ± 5% would make life interesting' (S20).
- Deflation: 'build it tomorrow, and tomorrow never comes' (S20).
